messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Imran had been 53 for a little over a year when he finally agreed to come in, a stocky South Asian man with paint still often ground into the lines of his hands and the habit of speaking carefully, as if choosing each sentence might keep something painful from spilling out. He lived with his wife and had spent most of his adult life as a painter, taking pride in the steady, physical work of making walls clean and homes livable. Long before he sought help, he had survived a period in his life when he was a civilian caught in a war zone, and he described that time as something that still did not fully make sense to him. He would say, in a flat voice at first, that one minute he had been going about ordinary errands and the next he was in a world where the sound of a bang could mean death, where a smell in the air could suddenly bring back the sharp, choking atmosphere of danger, and where there was no way to know what would happen next or how to stop it.

What he remembered most vividly was one particular episode in which an explosion occurred close enough that it left his body braced and thrown into a position he had never quite forgotten. When the memory came back now, he did not experience it as a calm picture from the past. He said it felt as though his body returned to the same position it had been in then, tense and frozen in place, with the same tightness in his muscles and the same helpless anticipation of what might follow. Sometimes the recollection would arrive suddenly while he was at work, and he would be standing on a ladder or bent over a wall, feeling for a moment as though he were back there again. He also spoke of the grief that came with remembering, a grief that could overwhelm him without warning, making him feel heavy and quiet for the rest of the day. At times he struggled to believe that something so extreme had really happened to him at all, as though the story belonged to someone else’s life, not his own.

In the years after he returned home, Imran tried to hold himself together by staying in motion. He threw himself into painting work, taking extra jobs and keeping busy from morning into the evening because, as he put it, “if I stop, I start thinking.” The thinking was often the same question, over and over: why had this happened to him, what had it meant, and whether there had been any point to surviving it. He could spend long stretches turning the event over in his mind, searching for an explanation that never satisfied him. At the same time, he made a habit of avoiding news reports about conflicts or attacks that sounded similar to what he had lived through. If a television in a shop or waiting room began showing such footage, he would turn away or leave the room, saying he did not want “to let it into my head.” The effort to keep himself occupied and away from reminders became part of his routine, though it also meant that he increasingly kept his world narrow and controlled.

Certain moments in his present life still hit him hard and without warning. The smell of something related to the war years could stop him in his tracks, bringing back the feeling of that time with a force that was difficult to explain to others. He noticed it most when he was working in people’s houses and encountered particular odors on the job, because a smell in a hallway or room could suddenly make him feel he was back in the war zone, scanning the air and trying to understand whether danger was near. Loud, explosive sounds were even harder. A slammed door, a dropped tool, or a bang from somewhere outside could make him jump before he had time to think, and he was embarrassed by how readily his body reacted when others around him barely noticed. He had become superalert in public and at work, constantly checking entrances, windows, and movement around him. He described feeling as if his body were always waiting for something to happen, tense and ready, even during ordinary conversations with his wife or while he was trying to concentrate on a paint line.

Over time, these experiences changed the way he saw himself and the world. Imran had once thought of painting as the thing that defined him: a skill he could rely on, a practical craft that gave him dignity and purpose. Now he feared that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had made him feel like himself. He still worked, but with less confidence and more strain, and there were days when the simple act of getting through a job felt like proof that his life had shrunk around him. He also said, without hesitation, that the world felt dangerous now, not just the place where he had once been trapped in war but the one he came home to as well. By the time he arrived for help, he was exhausted by the constant watchfulness, frustrated by his own startle reactions, and troubled by the sense that nothing in life felt meaningful anymore. He sought treatment because he could no longer keep pushing the memories aside, and because he was frightened that he might spend the rest of his life living as though danger were always one sound or one smell away.
